title: Out of The Woods
summary: Give back the rook to eliminate a dangerous passer, then use the active king to win the pawn race.

nodes.question: Must the attacked rook retreat?
nodes.explanation: White’s king attacks Rd8 and supports d7. Black can give up the rook for that pawn because its active king can then catch the b-pawn.

branches.title: Trade the rook for the dangerous pawn
commentary: Begin after White’s queen sacrifice, ...Rxd8 and Ke7. The preceding eight-piece promotion battle is source context.
Rxd7+ removes the dangerous passer with check and offers the rook. Calculate the pawn ending before declining the sacrifice.
Kxd7 accepts the rook. White has eliminated Black’s last piece, but its king is poorly placed for the remaining race.
Kc5 attacks b5 while keeping Black’s own pawn ready to advance.
b6 is the source’s selected attempt to save the pawn by pushing it.
Kxb6 catches that pawn. White’s king on d7 cannot defend b6.
Kd6 approaches the remaining d-pawn, trying to enter its path.
d4 starts the race with the white king behind the pawn. The exact resulting king-and-pawn ending is winning for Black; this branch stops at that checked endpoint.

branches.title: A rook retreat that gives White time
commentary: This independently selected alternative tests whether saving the rook preserves the result.
Ra8 gives away Black’s win and leaves White winning. Moving the rook is not automatically safer than exchanging it.

b6 is a checked winning reply. White keeps both passers alive and threatens b7 while the king on e7 supports d7. The selected endpoint is a White win, not an unverified general rule about all rook retreats.

branches.title: White promotes too soon after the retreat
commentary: Even after Black’s mistake, White still has to choose accurately. Compare b6 with immediate promotion.
Ra8 is losing for Black with best play: White can keep both passers with b6.
d8=Q instead throws away White’s win. The rook can capture the new queen along the eighth rank.
Rxd8 exchanges the rook for the d-pawn. This capture does not give check to the king on e7.
Kxd8 recaptures, but leaves White’s king too far from the b-pawn.
Kc5 attacks b5. The resulting pawn ending is a checked Black win, showing why White needed to keep both passers rather than rush promotion.

exercises.prompt: What matters more than keeping the rook?
exercises.answer: Eliminating d7 leaves Black’s king close enough to catch b5. The material sacrifice is justified by the exact resulting pawn ending.

exercises.prompt: Why does immediate promotion fail after ...Ra8?
exercises.answer: It lets the rook exchange itself for the d-pawn. White needs b6 to keep two promotion threats alive instead.
